facts.claim: George Loewenstein's 1994 information-gap account links curiosity to attention focused on missing knowledge.
facts.mechanism: Because awareness of a specific discrepancy between current and desired knowledge feels unresolved, people seek information that can close it.
facts.commonError: Curiosity is maximized by presenting a subject about which the audience knows absolutely nothing.

facts.claim: Sony introduced the TR-63 pocketable transistor radio in 1957.

facts.claim: John F. Kennedy announced the U.S. lunar landing-and-return goal to Congress on May 25, 1961.

facts.commonError: Kennedy's 1961 goal supplied NASA with a complete engineering plan for reaching the Moon.

facts.claim: Galileo first recorded Saturn's puzzling side structures in 1610, and Huygens explained a surrounding ring in 1659.
facts.mechanism: Because the apparent companions changed and disappeared with viewing angle, the observations created a mystery that better optics and a ring model could resolve.
facts.commonError: Galileo immediately identified Saturn's side structures as a thin flat ring.
facts.whyWrong: His telescope made the planet look triple or handled; the ring explanation came decades later from Huygens.

facts.claim: A useful surprise violates an audience prediction about the message's core rather than adding an unrelated shock.

facts.commonError: Any bizarre image improves a message even when it has no relationship to the point.
facts.whyWrong: Unrelated novelty may be remembered while the intended idea is forgotten or displaced.

facts.claim: A postdictable surprise becomes sensible after the missing explanation is supplied.

facts.commonError: The strongest surprise should remain arbitrary and inexplicable after the reveal.
facts.whyWrong: Permanent arbitrariness prevents the audience from updating a useful model and reduces the event to a gimmick.

facts.claim: Surprise captures attention briefly, whereas an information gap can hold attention until resolution.

facts.commonError: One startling opening guarantees that an audience will follow a long explanation.
facts.whyWrong: The initial prediction error does not supply an ongoing reason to listen once the momentary novelty passes.
